name: SkillCat
tagline: Mobile microlearning and certification prep for HVAC, electrical, plumbing and facilities technicians.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is a course player with quizzes, progress tracking and a certificate PDF at the end, which is genuinely a weekend build. What you cannot build is the thing people actually pay for: hundreds of hours of trade curriculum written by people who have been inside a rooftop unit, plus exam prep aligned to credentials like EPA 608 that an employer or an inspector will accept. A certificate you generated for yourself is worth exactly nothing to a hiring manager. There is also an employer side, where facilities and property management companies track who on the crew is trained on what, and that only works if the content is standardized across the whole team. A personal replacement answers a question nobody in this market is asking.
coreLoopDIY: A local study app that turns your own trade manuals and notes into lessons, quizzes and a spaced-repetition review queue with progress tracking.
requirements: Your own source material: manuals, code books, study guides, class notes
An LLM API key if you want auto-generated questions from PDFs
Node 20+ and a local machine to run it on
whatYouLose: Accredited or exam-aligned content, including EPA 608 prep that actually maps to the real test
Any credential an employer will recognize, because self-issued certificates are not credentials
Curriculum written by working tradespeople instead of guessed at by a model
The native mobile app, offline lessons and video, which is how people actually study on a job site
Employer-side tracking of who on a crew has completed what
moatNotes: The certificate only has value because someone other than you issues it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the product is the curriculum and the credibility of the credential, not the quiz engine. A technician studying for EPA 608 needs questions that resemble the actual exam and a certificate an employer will accept, and an employer paying for crew training needs a consistent, defensible record that their people were trained. Neither of those is a code problem. You can build a very nice personal study tool and still be in exactly the same position on test day.
notes: The course player is a weekend; the courses are not. The moat is licensed, exam-aligned trade curriculum plus a certificate that someone else vouches for.
prompt:
Build a local-first study app for skilled-trades material. Call it Bench.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite through better-sqlite3. No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. Single user, runs on localhost with `npm run dev`.

What it does:
1. Library: drop PDFs or Markdown files into a /content folder. On startup, index them into SQLite. For PDFs use pdf-parse to extract text and chunk it by page.
2. Decks: a deck is a named set of cards tied to one or more source documents. Let me create decks by hand and add cards manually.
3. Card generation: if OPENAI_API_KEY is set in .env, add a 'Generate cards' button on a document that sends chunks to the model and asks for multiple-choice and short-answer cards in strict JSON, each with the source page number. Show them in a review-before-save screen so I can edit or reject each one. If no key is set, hide the button entirely and do not fake it.
4. Study: spaced repetition using the SM-2 algorithm. Show one card at a time, grade 0-5, store the interval, ease and next due date. The home screen shows decks with due counts.
5. Every card links back to its source document and page so I can go read the real material.
6. Progress: a simple page with cards reviewed per day for the last 90 days and per-deck accuracy. Plain numbers and a bar chart, no dashboard theater.

Explicitly out of scope: video, certificates, any notion of passing or credentialing, multi-user, sharing, mobile apps, payments.

Put the API key in .env.example as OPENAI_API_KEY. Write the SQLite file to ./data/bench.db and gitignore ./data and ./content. Include a README with setup in under ten lines and a note that this issues no certificates and is not aligned to any real exam.
